The Federal Government says its new National Education Technology Strategy will help address the challenges of out-of-school children and teacher shortages through digital learning platforms, improved learner identification and expanded access to educational resources. The National Coordinator, Special Programmes Operation and Implementation Unit at the Federal Ministry of Education, Adebayo Onigbanjo, disclosed this in a press briefing in Abuja on Monday while outlining the strategy, which seeks to integrate 26 government initiatives into a unified digital education system. Onigbanjo said the initiatives were not designed to operate as separate projects but as interconnected interventions that would strengthen teaching, learning, education management, skills development and financing. He explained that the National Education Verification and Identification initiative would, “enable the government to map children and assign them unique Learner Identification Numbers, making it easier to identify those outside the education system and direct interventions towards them.” According to him, the data would support targeted programmes for out-of-school children, girls and learners enrolled in home education programmes. He said the Inspire Live initiative would connect pupils in schools without qualified subject teachers to certified teachers through digital platforms, while zero-rated data would remove internet subscription costs as a barrier to accessing online lessons. “The main message today is that these are not 26 separate projects; they form one connected system. The digital infrastructure is what connects them,” he said. Onigbanjo said the strategy would also link education with employment and entrepreneurship through programmes such as the Digital Training Academy, Technical and Vocational Education and Training and entrepreneurship initiatives. He explained that the strategy would be driven by five pillars, including data and interoperability, digital infrastructure, technology and procurement, teacher transformation and other measures aimed at strengthening education delivery. On data management, he said the government would build on the Nigeria Education Data Infrastructure by adopting common data standards that would allow existing education databases to exchange information automatically while preserving institutional autonomy. He said “priority would be given to data on schools, teachers, enrolment and education financing, with personal records protected under the Nigerian Data Protection Act.” On infrastructure, he said the government would prioritise reliable electricity, broadband connectivity and digital devices for schools, particularly in rural and underserved communities, while providing for the maintenance of such facilities. He added that the strategy would build on existing national connectivity initiatives, including Project BRIDGE and the Universal Service Provision Fund. COP31: Nigeria won’t sacrifice development for energy transition – FG How Innovation Is Reshaping the Global Online Gaming Industry FG raises W’Bank power loan to $1.25bn Onigbanjo said the government would also adopt vendor-neutral standards and transparent, performance-based procurement systems to encourage Nigerian developers to produce technology solutions aligned with the national curriculum. He said the National Teachers’ Digital Competency Framework would establish standards for teachers’ digital skills, certification and career progression, supported by a national teacher professional development portal. The strategy, he said, aligned with President Bola Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda and the Federal Ministry of Education’s vision of using education to drive national development, innovation and global competitiveness. He acknowledged the contributions of the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, state governments, development partners, the private sector, academia and civil society to the strategy’s development, particularly the Mastercard Foundation and the World Bank Group. The strategy comes against the backdrop of persistent challenges in Nigeria’s education sector, particularly the large population of children excluded from formal education and shortages of qualified teachers in public schools. A 2024 UNICEF report estimated that 18.3 million Nigerian children were out of school, comprising 10.2 million primary school-age children and 8.1 million of junior secondary school age. The Federal Ministry of Education, however, has cited an estimated 15 million out-of-school children in its recent interventions. The teacher shortage also remains a major concern. Data reported from the Federal Ministry of Education’s digital education database showed that 31.8 million learners in public schools were served by 592,077 teachers, representing a learner-teacher ratio of approximately 54 to one. The Universal Basic Education Commission has estimated that an additional 194,876 qualified teachers are needed in basic education. The strategy also builds on the Federal Government’s rollout of the Digital National Education Management Information System (DNEMIS), launched in July 2026 to improve education data collection, planning and accountability. As of its initial nationwide rollout, the platform had captured data from 124,548 schools, covering more than 40 million learners and 1.19 million teachers. The government says the new EdTech strategy will provide a coordinated framework for using technology to address these challenges and ensure that investments in digital education translate into improved learning outcomes.
